hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you really want something, do you tend to push too hard, or let it slide?
options: then you’ll know this monk. listen.
then he has something for you too. listen.
that’s honest. this story is about finding the middle.

steps.line: Sona grew up rich and sheltered, with soft, delicate feet. He became a monk, and was determined to wake up fast.
He walked in meditation day and night, pushing so hard his feet grew raw. Still nothing. “Maybe I should go home,” he thought, “and do good with my wealth.”

steps.q: The Buddha comes to see him. What do you think he asks?
o: “Didn’t you play the lute, back home?”
steps.why: A question about music, not meditation. Sona had played the vina, an Indian lute, back home, and the Buddha meets him there (Anguttara Nikaya 6.55).

steps.line: “Sona,” the Buddha asked, “when you lived at home, weren’t you good at the lute?” “Yes,” said Sona.
“When the strings were too tight, did it play well?” No. “Too loose?” No. “And when they were tuned just right?” “Then it played beautifully.”

steps.q: Why ask about a lute, instead of just telling Sona to ease off?
o: To test whether Sona was listening
He hoped Sona would go home and play
Sona already knew the answer, in his hands
steps.why: He didn’t need a new rule. He needed to remember what his fingers already knew.

steps.line: “Effort is the same,” the Buddha said. “Too much makes you restless. Too little makes you lazy. Find the tuning.” Sona did, and before long he woke up.

steps.q: Sona pushed until his feet bled. Why did the Buddha know that road so well?
o: He had starved himself nearly to death
He had walked barefoot across India
He had once been a lute player too
steps.why: Before waking up, the Buddha fasted so hard, the texts say, he could touch his spine through his belly. He gave it up, ate, and found the middle way.

steps.q: Notice: even a tuned string is still pulled tight. What does that say about effort?
o: The goal is no effort at all
Some pull is needed, just not too much
steps.why: A slack string makes no music. The middle way isn’t lazy: the Buddha still asked Sona for real, steady effort, just evenly tuned.

steps.line: Today, a late night at the desk, shoulders up by the ears. Or a whole weekend lost to the couch. Check your strings.
steps.label: today

say: this is the middle way, and the buddha’s whole teaching starts with it. in his first sermon, at the deer park, he named two extremes to avoid: chasing pleasure, like his palace life, and punishing the body, like the harsh fasting he had tried.

the idea grew in every school. the great mahayana thinker nagarjuna used the middle way for a path between saying things truly exist and saying nothing exists at all. his followers are still called the middle way school, madhyamaka.

steps.q: Once Sona woke up, he said a freed mind is like a mountain of solid rock. What can’t shake it?
steps.why: In the same sutta, Sona says sights, sounds and moods sweep by like wind from east, west, north and south, and the rock doesn’t move. The monk who nearly quit ends up a picture of steadiness.

today.say: today, check your tuning once an hour: jaw, shoulders, hands. if it’s too tight, let a little go. if it’s too loose, sit up and brighten. then carry on.
options: then today, tighten one string, just a little.

card.keepWhy: Not too tight, not too loose. Tune.
